title: Center for Brains, Minds and Machines
gist: This is the MIT CSAIL group page for the Center for Brains, Minds and Machines, which aims to build a computational understanding of human intelligence and an engineering practice from it. The page lists projects and news, with the latest item (October 13, 2026) on how artificial neural networks build their own learning machinery.

insights.claim: The Center for Brains, Minds and Machines at MIT CSAIL brings together computer scientists, cognitive scientists and neuroscientists to create a field called the Science and Engineering of Intelligence, aiming at a computational understanding of human intelligence and an engineering practice based on it.
insights.speaker: MIT CSAIL
entities: Center for Brains, Minds and Machines
insights.so_what: Neuroscience-informed AI research is one track in the field; slow-moving academic context rather than a near-term commercial signal.

insights.claim: The Orbit Metric Learning project uses sets of transforming examples as weak supervision to learn visual representations robust to changes in pose, scale and rotation that do not alter a scene's semantic category.
insights.speaker: MIT CSAIL
insights.so_what: Invariant representation learning with weak supervision may reduce labeled-data needs for vision systems.
insights.locator: Orbit Metric Learning: Weak Supervision for Invariant Representations

insights.claim: Spatio-temporal convolutional networks are a good model of how visual cortex represents the actions of others, and robustness to complex transformations is key to uncovering how human visual cortex is organized.
insights.speaker: MIT CSAIL
insights.so_what: Supports using deep vision models as neuroscience models, linking AI architecture choices to brain organization.
insights.locator: Spatio-temporal Convolutional Networks Explain Neural Representations of Human Action

insights.claim: A news item dated October 13, 2026 states that machine-learning networks can learn without detailed instructions from a designer, and that those that do may offer insight into how the brain reorganizes itself during learning.
insights.speaker: MIT CSAIL
insights.so_what: Only a teaser is present on this page; follow the full article for substance.
insights.locator: How artificial neural networks build their own learning machinery

insights.claim: CSAIL researchers developed a framework called the Canonical Representation Hypothesis for understanding how representations form in neural networks (March 31, 2025 news item).
insights.speaker: MIT CSAIL
insights.so_what: A theoretical framework in representation learning; background context.
